In algebraic geometry, the '''dimension of a scheme''' is a generalization of the [[dimension of an algebraic variety]]. [[Scheme theory]] emphasizes the [[Grothendieck's relative point of view|relative point of view]] and, accordingly, the '''relative dimension''' of a [[morphism of schemes]] is also important.

== Definition ==
By definition, the dimension of a scheme ''X'' is the dimension of the underlying [[topological space]]: the supremum of the lengths ''ℓ'' of chains of [[Irreducible space |irreducible]] closed subsets:
:<math>\emptyset \ne V_0 \subsetneq V_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq V_\ell \subset X.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Ch. I, just after Corollary 1.6.}}</ref>
In particular, if <math>X = \operatorname{Spec} A</math> is an [[affine scheme]], then such chains correspond to chains of [[prime ideal]]s (inclusion reversed), so the dimension of ''X'' is precisely the [[Krull dimension]] of ''A''.

If ''Y'' is an irreducible closed subset of a scheme ''X'', then the codimension of ''Y'' in ''X'' is the supremum of the lengths ''ℓ'' of chains of irreducible closed subsets:
:<math>Y = V_0 \subsetneq V_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq V_\ell \subset X.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Ch. II, just after Example 3.2.6.}}</ref>
An irreducible subset of ''X'' is an [[irreducible component]] of ''X'' if and only if its codimension in ''X'' is zero. If <math>X = \operatorname{Spec} A</math> is affine, then the codimension of ''Y'' in ''X'' is precisely the height of the prime ideal defining ''Y'' in ''X''.

== Examples ==
*If a finite-dimensional [[vector space]] ''V'' over a field is viewed as a scheme over the field,<ref group=note>The Spec of the [[symmetric algebra]] of the [[dual vector space]] of ''V'' is the scheme structure on <math>V</math>.</ref> then the dimension of the scheme ''V'' is the same as the vector-space dimension of ''V''.
*Let <math>X = \operatorname{Spec} k[x, y, z]/(xy, xz)</math>, ''k'' a field. Then it has dimension 2 (since it contains the [[hyperplane]] <math>H =
\{ x = 0 \} \subset \mathbb{A}^3</math> as an irreducible component). If ''x'' is a [[closed point]] of ''X'', then <math>\operatorname{codim}(x, X)</math> is 2 if ''x'' lies in ''H'' and is 1 if it is in <math>X - H</math>. Thus, <math>\operatorname{codim}(x, X)</math> for closed points ''x'' can vary.
*Let <math>X</math> be an algebraic pre-variety; i.e., an integral scheme [[scheme of finite type|of finite type]] over a field <math>k</math>. Then the dimension of <math>X</math> is the [[transcendence degree]] of the [[Function field (scheme theory)|function field]] <math>k(X)</math> of <math>X</math> over <math>k</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Ch. II, Exercise 3.20. (b)}}</ref> Also, if <math>U</math> is a nonempty open subset of <math>X</math>, then <math>\dim U = \dim X</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Ch. II, Exercise 3.20. (e)}}</ref>
*Let ''R'' be a [[discrete valuation ring]] and <math>X = \mathbb{A}^1_R = \operatorname{Spec}(R[t])</math> the affine line over it. Let <math>\pi: X \to \operatorname{Spec}R</math> be the projection. <math>\operatorname{Spec}(R) = \{ s, \eta \}</math> consists of 2 points, <math>s</math> corresponding to the [[maximal ideal]] and closed and <math>\eta</math> the zero ideal and open. Then the fibers <math>\pi^{-1}(s), \pi^{-1}(\eta)</math> are closed and open, respectively. We note that <math>\pi^{-1}(\eta)</math> has dimension one,<ref group=note>In fact, by definition, <math>\pi^{-1}(\eta)</math> is the fiber product of <math>\pi: X \to \operatorname{Spec}(R)</math> and <math>\eta = \operatorname{Spec}(k(\eta)) \to \operatorname{Spec} R</math> and so it is the Spec of <math>R[t] \otimes_R k(\eta) = k(\eta)[t]</math>.</ref> while <math>X</math> has dimension <math>2 = 1 + \dim R</math> and <math>\pi^{-1}(\eta)</math> is dense in <math>X</math>. Thus, the dimension of the closure of an open subset can be strictly bigger than that of the open set.
*Continuing the same example, let <math>\mathfrak{m}_R</math> be the maximal ideal of ''R'' and <math>\omega_R</math> a generator. We note that <math>R[t]</math> has height-two and height-one maximal ideals; namely, <math>\mathfrak{p}_1 = (\omega_R t - 1)</math> and <math>\mathfrak{p}_2 = </math> the kernel of <math>R[t] \to R/\mathfrak{m}_R, f \mapsto f(0) \bmod\mathfrak{m}_R</math>. The first ideal <math>\mathfrak{p}_1</math> is maximal since <math>R[t]/(\omega_R t - 1) = R[\omega_R^{-1}] = </math> the [[field of fractions]] of ''R''. Also, <math>\mathfrak{p}_1</math> has height one by [[Krull's principal ideal theorem]] and <math>\mathfrak{p}_2</math> has height two since <math>\mathfrak{m}_R[t] \subsetneq \mathfrak{p}_2</math>. Consequently,
:: <math>\operatorname{codim}(\mathfrak{p}_1, X) = 1, \, \operatorname{codim}(\mathfrak{p}_2, X) = 2,</math>
:while ''X'' is irreducible.<!-- The following is incomplete
== Relative dimension ==
The notion of a relative dimension is a common generalization of a dimension and a codimension (of schemes over a field). In literature, there does not appear to be the consensus on the definitions of a relative codimension of a scheme; this is because

Fulton's ''intersection theory'' uses the following definition: for a morphism of schemes <math>p: X \to S</math>, a closed integral subscheme <math>V \subset X</math>, the dimension of ''V'' over ''S'' is
:<math>\dim_S V = \operatorname{tr.deg.}(k(V)/k(T)) - \operatorname{codim}(T, S)</math>
where ''T'' is the closure of <math>p(V)</math>.-->

==Equidimensional scheme==
An '''equidimensional scheme''' (or, '''pure dimensional scheme''') is a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] whose [[irreducible component]]s are of the same [[Dimension (scheme)|dimension]] (implicitly assuming the dimensions are all well-defined).

===Examples===
All irreducible schemes are equidimensional.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Dundas | first1 = Bjorn Ian
 | last2 = Jahren | first2 = Björn
 | last3 = Levine | first3 = Marc |author-link3=Marc Levine (mathematician)
 | last4 = Østvær | first4 = P.A.
 | last5 = Röndigs | first5 = Oliver
 | last6 = Voevodsky | first6 = Vladimir |author-link6=Vladimir Voevodsky
 | isbn = 9783540458975
 | page = 101
 | publisher = Springer
 | title = Motivic Homotopy Theory: Lectures at a Summer School in Nordfjordeid, Norway, August 2002
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=gNErmkZzfKUC&pg=PA101
 | year = 2007}}.</ref>

In an [[affine space]], the union of a line and a point not on the line is ''not'' equidimensional. Generally, if two closed subschemes of some scheme, neither containing the other, have unequal dimensions, then their union is not equidimensional.

If a scheme is [[Smooth scheme|smooth]] (for instance, [[Étale morphism|étale]]) over Spec&nbsp;''k'' for some field&nbsp;''k'', then every [[Connected component (topology)|''connected'' component]] (which is then, in fact, an irreducible component) is equidimensional.

== Relative dimension ==
Let <math>f: X\rightarrow Y</math> be a [[morphism]] locally of [[Finite type scheme|finite type]] between two [[Scheme (mathematics)|schemes]] <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>. The relative dimension of <math>f</math> at a point <math>y \in Y</math> is the [[dimension]] of the [[Fiber (mathematics)|fiber]] <math>f^{-1} (y)</math>. If all the nonempty fibers {{clarify|general fiber?|date=June 2022}} are purely of the same dimension <math>n</math>, then one says that <math>f</math> is of relative dimension <math>n</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Adeel |first=Ahmed Kahn |date=March 2013 |title=Relative Dimension in Ncatlab |url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/relative+dimension |access-date=8 June 2022 |website=[[Ncatlab]]}}</ref>
